About 1 in 5 U.S. listings had a price cut in September. Realtor.com reports 20.8 percent of active listings had a reduction, up 0.9 points from a year earlier, while active inventory grew 5.4 percent to over 1,161,000 homes.

Illustrative: a $285,000 listing cut 4 percent sells for $273,600, which is $11,400 less than asked.

If a borrower's exit plan assumes the full list price, a lender can ask what payoff looks like at a lower sale price.

List price is an asking number, not a sale price.

What are banks reporting on commercial real estate loans? The Federal Reserve July 2026 loan officer survey covers the second quarter, and the answer depends on the loan type.

Nonfarm nonresidential: 13.2 percent of responding banks eased standards and 1.9 percent tightened.

Multifamily: 15.1 percent eased and 9.4 percent tightened.

Construction and land development: 25.9 percent of responding banks, 14 of 54, reported weaker demand.

Standards and demand differed by loan type, so a lender can compare each deal type against its own pipeline before reading one headline as the whole market.

posts.text:
A lender quotes 11 percent. On this loan, the real cost is higher.

Take $150,000 at 11 percent interest-only for 6 months, with 2.5 points paid at closing. Interest is $1,375 a month, or $8,250. The points add $3,750. Total cost: $12,000, which is 8 percent of the loan in half a year.

On a simple annualized basis, that is 16 percent: 11 percent interest plus 5 percent from the points. The CFPB describes APR as the interest rate plus additional fees.

Compare loans by total cost over the expected hold, not by the quoted rate alone.

vaultedonline.com
posts.alt: Bar showing the 6-month cost of a $150,000 loan at 11 percent interest-only with 2.5 points: $8,250 interest plus $3,750 points, $12,000 total. Cards show 11 percent quoted rate, plus 5 percent points annualized, 16 percent annualized cost.

posts.text:
Is hard money the same as private money? Sources disagree.

Scotsman Guide says the terms are often used interchangeably, yet calls hard money a subset of private lending: real estate-backed, short-term loans. CRE University, in 2009, called hard money lenders organized and usually licensed. A lender blog on BiggerPockets calls the terms completely interchangeable.

In 2022, AAPL and NPLA urged members to stop using "hard money" on their websites.

Takeaway: a label may not tell you the terms. Ask who funds the loan and what it costs.

vaultedonline.com

In 2022 AAPL and NPLA passed resolutions that urged members to cease using the term ‘hard money’ on their websites, marketing materials and communications.

The Census Bureau put the U.S. rental vacancy rate at 7.3 percent in the second quarter of 2026, against 7.0 percent a year earlier. Census calls that change not statistically different.

Why it matters for income-based underwriting: a higher assumed vacancy factor lowers net operating income. Per $100 of potential rent, a 5 percent vacancy factor leaves $95.00. At 7.3 percent it leaves $92.70, about 2.4 percent less.

Underwriters can assume different vacancy rates, 3 to 10 percent by one trade source. A national rate is not a local one.

posts.text:
Does your state tax the loan itself?

Some states charge a tax at recording that is generally based on the loan amount, not the property value.

Illustrative $400,000 loan:

Florida: note stamps of $0.35 per $100 come to $1,400. The intangible tax of 2 mills adds $800. Total: $2,200.

New York: mortgage recording taxes of 50, 25 and 25 cents per $100 add up to $4,000 (the last is 30 cents in some counties), before local taxes.

Same loan, very different tax line. Rates and rules vary by state, so lenders can ask title or counsel what applies.

posts.text:
Three draw request red flags a lender can check before paying.

1. The same invoice in more than one draw. Trinity describes one invoice submitted across multiple draws or projects.

2. An invoice altered to show higher quantities or prices.

3. A sub billing ahead of the work in place. Corpay describes this on progress payments.

One way to test this is comparing invoices with inspection findings. These tactics exploit gaps between documentation, inspections and draw approvals.

No single flag proves intent. It is a reason to ask a question.

posts.text:
A $180,000 loan at 12 percent defaults after 9 months. What sale price gets the lender whole?

Simple interest is $16,200. Add $9,000 in legal and carrying costs (illustrative) and the lender is owed $205,200.

Selling costs come off the top. One source puts seller closing costs at roughly 6 to 10 percent, used here as a proxy. At 8 percent, each sale dollar nets 92 cents, so breakeven is $205,200 / 0.92 = $223,044, about 124 percent of the loan. A $200,000 sale nets $184,000 and leaves the lender $21,200 short.

Lenders can run this math before setting LTV.

vaultedonline.com
posts.alt: Bar showing a $223,044 breakeven sale price built from $180,000 principal, $16,200 interest, $9,000 legal and carry, and $17,844 selling costs at 8 percent. Cards: $205,200 owed, 124 percent of the loan, and $21,200 short at a $200,000 sale. Illustrative.

posts.text:
Your borrower LLC is not on any sanctions list. Is it clear to lend? Not always.

OFAC, a Treasury office, publishes the SDN List, short for Specially Designated Nationals. Assets of listed persons are blocked, and US persons are generally prohibited from dealing with them.

The catch: an entity owned 50 percent or more in total by blocked persons is blocked too, even if its own name is not listed. Two blocked owners at 25 percent each count.

OFAC enforces civil penalties on a strict liability basis. Lenders can screen borrowers and their owners before closing.
posts.alt: Diagram of OFAC's 50 percent rule example: Blocked Person X owns 25 percent and Blocked Person Y owns another 25 percent of Entity A, so the 50 percent total makes Entity A blocked even if not named on the SDN List. Takeaway: lenders can screen borrowers and their owners.

posts.text:
A borrower wants to refinance, but a second lender already holds a lien on the property. Now what?

The new lender may ask that second lender to sign a subordination agreement. One lienholder agrees to lower the priority of its lien so that another lien moves ahead of it.

Why? If the second lender does not sign, the new lender might not refinance. The cost to the lender stepping back: subordinate liens might not get paid after a foreclosure.

Takeaway: a lender asked to subordinate can first check what sits ahead of it.

vaultedonline.com
posts.alt: Before and after lien order. Before: existing first lien is position 1, second lien is position 2. After the subordination agreement: new refinance loan is position 1, second lien is lowered to position 2. Notes: the new lender might not refinance without it; subordinate liens might not get paid after a foreclosure.

sources.quote: A "subordination agreement" is a contract to prioritize one debt over another for repayment. ... the new lender might not refinance the first mortgage. ... subordinate (low priority) liens might not get paid after a foreclosure.

posts.text:
A fund raises $5,000,000 at a 7 percent cost and lends it all at an 11.5 percent yield. What is left?

The difference is the spread: 11.5 minus 7 is 4.5 percentage points. On $5,000,000, that is $575,000 of interest earned against $350,000 owed, or $225,000 a year before expenses and losses.

Now the cost of capital rises one point to 8 percent. The spread shrinks to 3.5 points, or $175,000. One point on the cost side removed about 22 percent of the spread income.

Lenders can compare the spread, not just the loan rate, when they price new loans.

vaultedonline.com
posts.alt: Graphic for an illustrative $5,000,000 fund. Cards show $575,000 interest earned at an 11.5 percent yield, $350,000 owed at a 7 percent cost, and $225,000 of spread. Two bars show the spread falling from 4.5 to 3.5 points when cost rises to 8 percent, a $50,000 drop.

sources.title: Net interest spread
sources.quote: Net interest spread is expressed as interest yield on earning assets (any asset, such as a loan, that generates interest income) minus interest rates paid on borrowed funds.

sources.title: Net Interest Margin and Spread Analysis
sources.quote: Interest Spread = (Yield on Interest-Earning Assets) – (Cost of Interest-Bearing Liabilities)

posts.text:
Moving loan servicing out of the house does not move every responsibility with it.

For residential mortgages, Freddie Mac describes a servicer as the main point of contact, one that collects payments, passes them to the lender, and funds escrow for tax and insurance bills.

For banks, regulators add the other side. Joint guidance says using third parties does not diminish a banking organization responsibility to meet its requirements. Private lender rules vary.

Before choosing, a lender can write down what the servicer will do and what stays with the lender.

sources.title: Interagency Guidance on Third-Party Relationships

posts.text:
A borrower defaults on a rental loan. Tenants still pay the borrower. Can the lender collect that rent instead?

That is the job of an assignment of rents. The borrower assigns the rents to the lender, and the lender grants the borrower a license to collect them. One law firm calls that license revocable upon default.

After default, enforcement generally requires added steps, which may include notice to the borrower and direction letters to tenants. The clause is not self-executing in many states, and receivership is a common enforcement tool.

Lenders can ask counsel how it works locally.

vaultedonline.com
posts.alt: Three step cards: rents assigned to the lender with a license for the borrower to collect, license revocable upon default, then notice and direction letters to tenants. A panel says the clause varies by state and is not self-executing in many states.

sources.title: Understanding the Rents, Issues, and Profits Clause in Mortgage Lending
sources.quote: The clause is not self-executing in many states. Other jurisdictions rely on case law, which may require judicial intervention or receivership before the lender may collect. Per the page: enforcement generally requires additional steps, which may include providing notice to the borrower, serving direction letters on tenants, revoking the borrower's license to collect.

Percent complete: an inspector verifies the job is 50 percent done, so $60,000 is earned (50 percent x $120,000).

Milestone: money is tied to checkpoints. Picture four hypothetical checkpoints of $30,000 each. If the work is 50 percent done but only the first checkpoint is verified, $30,000 is released.

Both are meant to follow verified work, not the calendar. Lenders can spell out in the loan documents which method applies and how partial work is treated.

posts.text:
What does a final draw wait on? Two lender guides name overlapping items.

A hard money guide says the last draw "usually requires final inspection, a certificate of occupancy, and a final lien waiver." A commercial construction guide lists a certificate of occupancy, final unconditional lien waivers from all tiers, and a final title endorsement with no open liens.

Requirements vary by lender, loan and state.

Lenders can share the final draw list with the borrower early, so the last release is not waiting on paperwork.

posts.text:
How many mortgages are slipping 90 days late? The New York Fed's Q2 2026 household debt report, released August 11, 2026, has a number worth knowing.

The annualized share of mortgage balances newly becoming 90 or more days late was 1.52 percent, up from 1.29 percent a year earlier. That is 0.23 points, or about 18 percent higher.

These are household mortgages in general, not private loans, and $505 billion of new mortgage debt was originated in the quarter.

Lenders can treat it as a backdrop, then check their own loans one by one.

posts.text:
A borrower stops paying the property tax bill, and the lender pays it. What happens to the loan?

That payment is called a protective advance: money a lender pays for an expense the borrower was supposed to cover, such as delinquent property taxes or lapsed hazard insurance. One source says it gets added to the loan balance and accrues interest.

Illustrative: a $250,000 loan on a $350,000 value is 71.4 percent LTV. Add a $6,500 advance and the balance is $256,500, or 73.3 percent.

Lenders can recheck LTV after any advance. Terms vary by lender and state.

vaultedonline.com
posts.alt: Two bars compare an illustrative $250,000 loan on a $350,000 property before and after a $6,500 protective advance. LTV rises from 71.4 percent to 73.3 percent as the balance grows to $256,500.

sources.title: Protective Advances: Definition, Rules, and Borrower Rights
sources.quote: A protective advance is a payment made by a lender to cover an expense the borrower was supposed to cover. These advances get added to your loan balance and accrue interest.

sources.quote: All sums advanced for the purpose of payment of real estate taxes ... insurance premiums, other items ... reasonably necessary to protect the Collateral from forfeiture, casualty, loss or waste. (page undated, accessed 2026-10-25)

posts.text:
Two loans default on the same day, in two different states. One lender must file a lawsuit. The other may not need a court at all.

That is the gap between judicial and nonjudicial foreclosure. In a judicial state, a court oversees the case, and Nolo says it can last several months or even years in some cases. In a nonjudicial state, a trustee typically handles it, and Nolo says it can take just a few months or less.

Procedures differ widely by state. Lenders can ask counsel which process applies to a loan.

vaultedonline.com
posts.alt: Two comparison cards. Judicial: the lender must file a lawsuit, a court oversees through hearings, and it can take several months or even years in some cases. Nonjudicial: power of sale with no court order first, a trustee typically handles it, and it often takes a few months or less. Varies by state.

sources.title: The Difference Between a Judicial and Nonjudicial Foreclosure
sources.quote: In states with a judicial foreclosure process, the lender must file a lawsuit to foreclose. The court system usually isn't involved in states that permit a nonjudicial foreclosure process. A trustee typically handles a nonjudicial foreclosure. The judicial foreclosure process can be lengthy, frequently lasting several months or even years in some cases. Nonjudicial foreclosure procedures differ widely from state to state. (page undated, accessed 2026-10-25; the nonjudicial process is often quicker, "often lasting just a few months or less.")

sources.title: non-judicial foreclosure
sources.quote: A non-judicial foreclosure is when lenders foreclose property without getting a court order first. (Last reviewed in August of 2023 by the Wex Definitions Team.)

posts.text:
What should be in a private loan file on closing day, and on payoff day?

At closing, a file can hold the signed note, the deed of trust or mortgage, any guaranty, the business purpose certification and the entity certificate, among others.

A servicer boarding checklist lists the title policy, the insurance declarations page, the most recent tax bill and the borrower payment history.

At payoff, FDIC guidance says a lender should provide a recordable lien release. For consumer mortgages, the CFPB says the original note should be returned and the release may be delayed.

Varies by lender and state.

vaultedonline.com
posts.alt: Three checklist columns. At closing: signed note, deed of trust or mortgage, guaranty, business purpose certification, entity certificate. During the loan: title policy, insurance declarations page, tax bill, payment history. At payoff: recordable lien release, original note returned, release may be delayed.

posts.text:
Illustrative: one $210,000 loan. Two exits. Two different ways the lender gets repaid.

Flip: the house sells at its $300,000 after-repair value. Selling costs of 6 percent take $18,000, leaving $282,000. That is $72,000 above the loan, before interest and other costs.

Hold: a refinance repays the loan, and the new lender looks at rent. With $2,400 rent, a $2,050 payment gives 1.17 coverage. A $2,600 payment gives 0.92, under a 1.0 floor one lender cites, so the refinance may not work.

Lenders can ask which exit is planned, then test it with that exit's own numbers.

posts.text:
A borrower in default offers to hand over the property instead of facing foreclosure. That is a deed in lieu of foreclosure: the borrower conveys the property to the lender.

One source says the lender who accepts takes title subject to all liens and claims affecting the property. A deed in lieu does not wipe out junior liens the way a foreclosure can.

One source says a lender should hesitate before accepting where junior liens or judgments are outstanding. Some may choose foreclosure for clean title. Varies by state.

Check what sits on title before deciding.
